summary: Summarizes how hashes are used in many Internet protocols and discusses how newly found collision attacks do or do not affect them. It shows how to thwart known attacks on digital certificates and outlines directions for protocol designers. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains what attacks on MD5 and SHA-1 can do to Internet protocols. It finds that collision attacks mainly affect some uses of digital signatures, while many other hash uses are not affected in the same way.

subtitle: How collision attacks on MD5 and SHA-1 affect different uses of hashes in Internet protocols.

tldr.problem: Published attacks on MD5 and SHA-1 prompted concern that Internet protocols using these hashes might be broken. The risks differ according to how a protocol uses a hash.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC distinguishes collision attacks from pre-image attacks, reviews common protocol uses, and analyzes signatures and certificates in detail.
tldr.outcome: The authors agree protocols should support changing hash algorithms, but disagree on how quickly to move to SHA-256. They recommend an orderly move away from MD5 and SHA-1, especially MD5.

sections.title: What Hash Attacks Break
sections.content:
A hash turns a message of any size into a fixed-size value. A collision attack finds two different messages with the same hash. A first-preimage attack finds a message matching a known hash, while a second-preimage attack finds a different message matching a given message's hash.

The attacks known to be practical or almost practical against MD5 and SHA-1 at the time of this RFC were collision attacks. The RFC notes that these attacks require at least one message to have a useful structure, which makes a real-world attack harder than merely finding any collision.
sections.plainLanguage: A collision attack makes two different messages share one hash value. A pre-image attack starts with a hash or a message and finds matching data, which the RFC treats as a different and more serious class of attack.

sections.title: How Protocols Use Hashes
sections.content:
Internet protocols use hashes for message and certificate signatures, challenge-response exchanges, shared-secret authentication, key derivation, mixing data, and checking files against a hash received separately. The RFC says collision attacks affect only the first two categories, and even those uses are affected in limited circumstances.

For challenge-response and shared-secret authentication, the authors say the available attacks are generally not considered sensible because the attacker cannot choose the secret being authenticated. IETF key derivation functions also use random input from both parties, which prevents an attacker from structuring the hashed message.
sections.plainLanguage: The risk depends on who chooses the data before it is hashed and signed. The RFC says many hash uses do not give an attacker the control needed to exploit a collision.

sections.title: Signatures and Certificates
sections.content:
In a collision attack on a signature, an attacker prepares two messages with the same hash, gets one signed, and then presents the signature with the other. When a person evaluates a signed authorization, keeping the original signed message can expose the substitution. Automated systems, such as electronic data interchange, require detailed evaluation because they may act without a person checking the message.

For certificates, the described attack required predicting certificate contents before issuance, including identity, serial number, and validity dates. The RFC says certificate issuers can make signed fields less predictable, for example by making part of a serial number unpredictable or adding a random component to the identity.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature can be misused if an attacker prepares two documents with the same hash and gets one signed. Keeping the exact signed document helps reveal a substitution; automated systems need their own analysis.

sections.title: Migration and Protocol Design
sections.content:
The two authors disagree about whether protocols should migrate to SHA-256 immediately. One argues that attacks improve and a move should happen before a crisis. The other says the known attacks had not shown discernible real-world effects and that changing algorithms can cause interoperability problems.

Both authors agree that protocols should support longer hash values and be able to change cryptographic algorithms. The RFC also says a practical pre-image attack would have a serious effect on many protocols, while the known pre-image attacks discussed in the document were not practical.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors disagree about the timing of a switch to SHA-256. They agree that protocols should be designed so their cryptographic algorithms can be changed.

sections.title: The RFC's Security Assumption
sections.content: The security discussion assumes that the attacks against hashes used in Internet protocols are collision attacks. It notes that significant pre-image attacks had been found, but were not practical at the time. A pre-image attack that is financially or computationally impractical is different from one an attacker could carry out in a useful time and at a meaningful cost.
sections.plainLanguage: The conclusions depend on the attacks known when this RFC was written. The authors warn that a practical pre-image attack would change the risk assessment.
